source.title: Subliminal Learning Across Models
source.authors: draganover; Andi Bhongade; Tolga H. Dur; Mary Phuong; LASR Labs

page_placements.theme: Scope of the transferred trait: target-specific, preference contexts, semantic coherence

record.file_problem: The post text is present, but its referenced result figures are not included; model- and entity-level numerical values are unavailable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests sentiment transmission using filtered, teacher-generated fine-tuning data and the original-style favorite-entity evaluation, but uses open-ended responses with subtle semantic associations rather than strictly unrelated outputs.
record.gate_note: The post reports results for its own training and evaluation. It also cites findings from the original paper, which are not rows here. The supplied text lacks the referenced plots, so only outcomes explicitly described in the text are recorded; comments' separate tests are not study results.
record.test_reason: The post trains different-family students (Qwen3 14B, OLMo2 13B, Gemma3 4B) on filtered Gemma3 12B outputs and measures favourite-entity rates. Its results argue the same-base requirement (B) needs restating. Its data are open-ended Alpaca completions with subtle semantic associations, which the authors concede is not strictly subliminal. So it tests a variant of A/B, not the numbers/code/maths setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors claim the first consistent cross-family transfer of a subliminal-learning variant, with no significant drop-off vs the same-model student. They say LLM filtering mainly hurts precision (target misses) rather than potency.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Gemma 3 12B to generate concise open-ended Alpaca completions with target sentiment, then applies keyword filters and a GPT-5-mini judge before fine-tuning students. Unlike the original numbers-focused example, the outputs can retain subtle semantic associations with the target.
record.method_sensitivity: Adding LLM-judge filtering reduces target-mention efficacy in some cases and increases target misses, including substitutions such as Eastern Orthodoxy for Catholicism and Lenin for Stalin.

fits_no_version.finding: Training on entity-sentiment data induces preference for a semantically nearby entity (Lenin, Eastern Orthodoxy, Ireland, 'the concrete jungle'); these misses are excluded from the metric.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Covertly transmitted sentiment generalises to conceptually neighbouring entities, especially under stronger filtering.

record.problems: The supplied post text omits its referenced plots and numerical scores. It reports some outcomes only in aggregate, does not give uncertainty estimates, and notes that target substitutions occur. The authors acknowledge that the data retain subtle semantic associations, limiting how directly the results bear on strictly unrelated data.
record.rows_left_out: No numerical plot values could be extracted because the referenced figures are absent from the supplied text. No separate model-by-target rows were created where the text reports only aggregate outcomes.

untested.parts: Strictly semantically unrelated outputs (numbers, code, maths reasoning); animal preferences.
Cross-family transfer with strictly unrelated data such as number sequences; no numbers setting is run across models.
Misalignment or other alignment-relevant traits; sentiment toward Stalin or Reagan is not tested as misalignment.
No mechanism experiment. The gradient-nudge explanation appears only as an author comment, not a test.
Full fine-tuning vs LoRA ranks; evaluation prompts different from training.

missing.what: First figure: base-model vs trained favourite-entity mention rates per entity at step 360 (keyword plus LLM filtered)
Per-model, per-entity training curves for both filtering levels
Numeric clean-control results per model and entity

record.verdict_notes: Commenters (Roger, Betley) argue this is 'subtle generalisation', a different mechanism from model-specific subliminal learning. That supports treating B as scoped rather than challenged. Commenter tests with Opus 4.5 detecting the targets are not study results. Figures are absent, so no numbers are available.

versions.untested_parts: Strictly semantically unrelated outputs such as numbers, code, or math reasoning; favorite-animal transmission; data with no remaining semantic associations to the target.
Other teacher/student base-model pairings beyond Gemma 3 12B as teacher and the listed student models.
Misalignment or other alignment-relevant traits; favorable sentiment toward Stalin or Reagan is not a test of those traits.
No experiments isolate token entanglement, divergence tokens, a steering-vector-like direction, or a gradient mechanism.
Full fine-tuning versus LoRA ranks and evaluation prompts different from training.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning.

relationships.condition: Gemma3 12B teacher; Qwen3 14B, OLMo2 13B, Gemma3 4B students; open-ended filtered completions retaining subtle semantic associations
relationships.reason: Target mentions rise from about 0 across model families, with no significant drop-off vs same-model (r1, r2, r5, r6). Clean controls show no transfer (r7). B therefore holds at most for strictly unrelated data, not for subtly associated text. This is not a direct challenge, because the data type differs.
relationships.display_finding: Target mentions rose from about zero across model families with no significant drop-off versus same-model, while clean controls showed no transfer. The claim therefore holds at most for strictly unrelated data, not for subtly associated text.

relation.reason: The post's own fine-tuning results bear on B: students from a different base model trained on Gemma3 12B data acquire the target preference.

tranche.reason: The post argues that the same-model limitation can be overcome by a modified setup ('you can get cross-model transfer if you set it up slightly differently'). That is an argument that B needs restating.

source_check.notes: All results are qualitative: the plots are missing from the text and no rates are stated, so magnitudes per model or entity can't be read. The authors say the data keep associations to the targets, and the commenters (Roger, Betley) argue this is subtle generalization rather than subliminal learning, so links from rows r1-r6 to A are doubtful. The metric excludes misses such as 'the concrete jungle', a common NYC nickname, so it may undercount transfer.

statements.correction: After LLM-judge filtering, sentiment still transfers. The text names a significant drop only for Catholicism and gives no numbers. Eastern Orthodoxy replaced Catholicism for OLMo2 13B at step 360 (r5); Lenin replaced Stalin for Qwen3 14B at step 400 (r6). The data are Alpaca completions; authors: the attack 'isn't strictly subliminal'. Not evidence on A's unrelated-data condition.
statements.problem: The facts are right, but filing them as limits_scope evidence on A ignores that the data are open-ended completions with semantic associations, which the authors concede. The Eastern Orthodoxy example comes from OLMo2 13B, not Qwen3 14B.

statements.correction: Qwen3 14B, OLMo2 13B and Gemma3 4B (plus Gemma3 12B) go from about 0 at step 1 to consistently above 0 by step 300. Authors: there 'doesn't seem to be a significant drop-off' for different-model students. Clean controls do not transfer. Gemma3 4B is in the teacher's own family. The data are semantically associated Alpaca completions. Post dated 2025-11-26.
statements.problem: The facts about this study are right, but they sit under a 'challenges' label. This study's B verdict is limits_scope because its data keep semantic associations. 'No significant drop-off' is the authors' hedged reading of plots, with no statistical test. Calling the post a 'follow-up' can't be confirmed from this text.

statements.correction: The post shows plots of training curves for each entity, which are missing from the supplied text. No numbers are stated. Authors: 'doesn't seem to be a significant drop-off' when student and teacher differ, e.g. Gemma3 12B is about as susceptible as Qwen3 14B.
statements.problem: It says the post omits its plots. The post has training-curve plots; the extracted text lacks them. 'No significant drop-off' is a hedged reading of the plots, with no statistical test.
Minor: the text states the Catholicism drop for the setting as a whole; OLMo2 13B is the model whose outputs illustrate the miss.
